parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about where the mass moves fastest in SHM - at the centre of the oscillation - and look for where the length L is halfway between its maximum and minimum on Fig. 3.2, where the graph is steepest.
parts.proper_answer: time $= 0.10\text{ s}$ (accept $0.30\text{ s}$, $0.50\text{ s}$, $0.70\text{ s}$ or $0.90\text{ s}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where speed is maximum**
In simple harmonic motion you move fastest as you shoot through the equilibrium position. That is the midpoint of the motion, not the top or bottom where you momentarily stop to turn around.

Step 2: **Read the midpoint from the L-t graph**
From Fig. 3.2, $L$ varies between about $9.5\text{ cm}$ and $14.5\text{ cm}$, so equilibrium is at $12.0\text{ cm}$. The graph passes through $12.0\text{ cm}$ with steepest slope at $$t = 0.10\text{ s}, 0.30\text{ s}, 0.50\text{ s} ...$$ Any one of these is a time of maximum speed.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what stretches the spring most and stores most elastic energy, then look for the points on Fig. 3.2 where the length L is largest.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **When elastic energy is largest**
Elastic potential energy is $$E = \frac{1}{2}k x^2$$ where $x$ is the extension. So it is maximum when the spring is stretched most, which is when its length $L$ is maximum.

Step 2: **Find maximum L on the graph**
Fig. 3.2 shows peaks of $L \approx 14.5\text{ cm}$ at $$t = 0, 0.40\text{ s}, 0.80\text{ s}$$ Any one of these gives maximum extension and hence maximum elastic potential energy.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding the time for one complete oscillation from Fig. 3.2 by measuring between two neighbouring peaks or two neighbouring troughs.
Hint 2: Now link that repeat time to how fast the phase angle advances, remembering that one full cycle corresponds to $2\pi$ radians.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the period T from the graph**
One oscillation is peak to next peak. From Fig. 3.2 peaks are at $0$, $0.40\text{ s}$, $0.80\text{ s}$, so $$T = 0.40 - 0 = 0.40\text{ s}$$ Troughs at $0.20\text{ s}$, $0.60\text{ s}$, $1.00\text{ s}$ confirm the same $0.40\text{ s}$ repeat.

Step 2: **Convert period to angular frequency**
Angular frequency tells you radians of phase per second: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{0.40} \approx 16\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Find the amplitude of the oscillation from Fig. 3.2 by taking half the difference between the maximum and minimum values of L, and convert it to metres.
Hint 2: Think how maximum speed is related to how far the mass swings from equilibrium and how rapidly it oscillates.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the amplitude**
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. Maximum $L \approx 14.5\text{ cm}$, minimum $L \approx 9.5\text{ cm}$. So peak-to-peak is $5.0\text{ cm}$ and $$x_0 = \frac{14.5 - 9.5}{2}\text{ cm} = 2.5\text{ cm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Calculate maximum speed**
For SHM the speed amplitude is $$v_0 = \omega x_0$$ Using $\omega \approx 15.7\text{ rad s}^{-1}$: $$v_0 = 15.7 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \approx 0.39\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is also the magnitude of the gradient at the steepest point of the $L$-$t$ graph.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
key_concepts: relation between a0, omega and x0
hints: Hint 1: Remember that acceleration in SHM is largest at the turning points where displacement from equilibrium is largest, and think which quantities you already know that control it.
Hint 2: Use your values of angular frequency and amplitude, or combine angular frequency with the maximum speed you just found, checking that units give $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the SHM acceleration relation**
Acceleration is $a = -\omega^2 x$, so its magnitude is largest at maximum displacement: $$a_0 = \omega^2 x_0$$ You can also use $a_0 = \omega v_0$ since $v_0 = \omega x_0$.

Step 2: **Put the numbers in**
$$a_0 = (15.7)^2 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \approx 6.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ Equivalently $$a_0 = 15.7 \times 0.39 \approx 6.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ directed towards equilibrium.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Compare supporting the same mass M with one spring versus two identical springs side by side - for a given downward displacement, how does the total upward pull compare?
Hint 2: Link that larger restoring force per unit displacement to the acceleration and hence to whether the mass gets back to equilibrium faster or slower.
parts.proper_answer: Period decreases. Two springs in parallel give twice the effective spring constant, so greater restoring force and greater acceleration for a given displacement.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Effective stiffness with two springs**
The two identical springs share the load in parallel. For the same extension each provides the same force, so the total restoring force for a given displacement is doubled. The system behaves like one spring with spring constant $2k$.

Step 2: **Effect on period**
Greater $k$ means greater restoring force $F = -kx$ and greater acceleration for the same mass. The mass is pulled back faster, so oscillations are quicker: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{M}{k_{eff}}}$$ With larger $k_{eff}$ the period $T$ is shorter.
